Q: How to convert date to dd/mm/yy in Excel? A:

Try this

Jan 3, 2022 8:00:00 PM GMT

=TEXT(DATE(MID(A1,FIND(",",A1)+2,4),MATCH(LEFT(A1,3),{"Jan","Feb","Mar","Apr","May","Jun","Jul","Aug","Sep","Oct","Nov","Dec"},0),MID(A1,5,FIND(",",A1)-5)),"dd/mm/yy")

Explanation:

1. Extract month

LEFT(A1, 3)

MATCH(LEFT(A1,3), {"Jan","Feb","Mar","Apr","May","Jun","Jul","Aug","Sep","Oct","Nov","Dec"}, 0)

This returns 1

2. Extract Day

FIND(",", A1)

MID(A1, 5, FIND(",",A1) - 5)

3. Extract Year

FIND(",", A1) + 2

MID(A1, FIND(",",A1) + 2, 4)

4. then build a date

DATE(year, month, day)

5. Finally format the date

=TEXT(DATE(...), "dd/mm/yy")

Q: How to create Amazon SES identity verification CNAME records in Route 53 across different AWS accounts using CDK? A:

CrossAccountZoneDelegationRecord is not the right construct here. It only exists for delegating subdomains by writing NS records in the parent zone, not for creating arbitrary records like the SES DKIM CNAMEs.

For this setup, the usual approach is:

  • create the SES identity in the Email Account

  • get the DKIM tokens generated by SES

  • create the corresponding CNAME records in the hosted zone that lives in the DNS Account

Since the hosted zone is in a different account, CDK will not do that automatically for you. The simplest way to handle it programmatically is with a custom resource.

In practice:

  1. In the DNS Account, create an IAM role that allows:

    • route53:ChangeResourceRecordSets on the hosted zone

    • optionally route53:ListResourceRecordSets if needed

  2. Trust that role from the Email Account

  3. In the Email Account CDK stack:

    • create the SES domain identity

    • use a Lambda-backed custom resource or AwsCustomResource

    • assume the role in the DNS account

    • call ChangeResourceRecordSets to UPSERT the SES DKIM CNAME records

So the flow is basically:

  • SES identity is created in account A

  • Route 53 records are written in account B through an assumed role

That is the standard cross-account solution.

Roughly:

const identity = new ses.EmailIdentity(this, "Identity", {
  identity: ses.Identity.domain("example.com"),
});

new cr.AwsCustomResource(this, "SesDkimRecords", {
  onCreate: {
    service: "Route53",
    action: "changeResourceRecordSets",
    parameters: {
      HostedZoneId: hostedZoneId,
      ChangeBatch: {
        Changes: dkimRecords.map((r) => ({
          Action: "UPSERT",
          ResourceRecordSet: {
            Name: r.name,
            Type: "CNAME",
            TTL: 300,
            ResourceRecords: [{ Value: r.value }],
          },
        })),
      },
    },
    assumedRoleArn: dnsAccountRoleArn,
    physicalResourceId: cr.PhysicalResourceId.of("ses-dkim-records"),
  },
  policy: cr.AwsCustomResourcePolicy.fromSdkCalls({
    resources: cr.AwsCustomResourcePolicy.ANY_RESOURCE,
  }),
});

The main point is that you need to handle the Route 53 change yourself through a cross-account role. There is no built-in CDK construct for “cross-account CNAME record creation” similar to CrossAccountZoneDelegationRecord.

Also, if you are troubleshooting the final SES setup, it helps to verify that the DKIM/SPF/DMARC records are actually visible and correct after deployment. A tool like https://emaildnscheck.com/ can be useful for that.

So the short answer is: use a custom resource + cross-account IAM role + Route 53 ChangeResourceRecordSets API call.

Q: How to restart a Docker Compose service if it stops producing stdout for 5 minutes? A:

The idiomatic way to do it, I think, is to have the container report an unhealthy status if it hasn't produced any output for 10 minutes. Then have some monitoring software running that restarts unhealthy containers.

A way to do a health check could be to pipe the output through a small program that updates a timestamp whenever you write to the log. Then the health check can check if the timestamp is more than 10 minutes old.

Q: What is the source of the double-dollar sign selector query function in Chrome/Firefox? A:

Yes, it’s added by dev tools, and no, it’s not for internal usage, but for your debugging.

It’s one part of what Chromium calls its Console Utilities API, and it’s what Firefox calls a Web Console Helper.

The history behind the “name”

In case you want to know about this specific part (function), the following is an update/cleanup of Paul Irish’s fellow answer.

Most of these helpers originate from Firebug’s Command Line API. Nowadays we just have parity across browsers because Firebug did things (mostly) right.

But back when Firebug was being created (2006), the JavaScript library that was all the rage was Prototype.js. $ was grabbed by Prototype for some getElementById() syntactic sugar as that was certainly the quickest way to be grabbing elements and most common element acquisition technique at the time. (It was such a timesaver that folks used the whole library just for the $ sugar.)

In early 2006, jQuery then debuted and used $() for selecting any element based on its CSS selector. As this CSS Selector Engine Timeline post shows, Prototype then followed up four days later with their own, but as $ was already taken in their library, they just went to $$(), which is now known as the bling-bling function.

So Firebug was leveraging Prototype's API as it was still ruling the roost in 2006. Now (in the days of jQuery and post-jQuery aliasing like window.$ = document.querySelectorAll.bind(document)), we see it as quite backwards. (Interestingly, Opera Dragonfly had chosen $ as their querySelectorAll alias, to better match present-day practices, which IMO makes a bit more sense.)
